name: Testosterone undecanoate injection (Aveed)

lead: Testosterone undecanoate injection is a long-acting testosterone depot sold as Aveed in the US and Nebido in Europe. It is given in a medical setting to men with testosterone deficiency, and people on TRT discuss it as a way to avoid frequent self-injection while keeping the usual muscle and lean-mass benefits.

The chain: the ester dissolves in oil and releases slowly from the muscle depot, where it is converted to testosterone; reported intramuscular half-life is around 21 days in tea seed oil and 34 days in castor oil. Registered studies cover long-term safety, blood pressure and other outcomes in hypogonadal men. None examine cosmetic outcomes.

paras: It is administered by a clinician at intervals of weeks to months, so visits replace daily or weekly routines. Aveed requires observation after injection under its safety programme.

The FDA rejected Aveed in 2008, 2009 and 2013 over pulmonary oil microembolism (POME) and anaphylaxis concerns before approving it in 2014 with a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy. Other reported effects are acne, hypertension, raised liver enzymes and lipid changes. It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US.

angle.text: Aveed is a long-acting, clinic-administered testosterone injection for diagnosed deficiency, appealing to people who want infrequent dosing. The looks link is the usual TRT one, more lean mass and less fat, studied in men with low testosterone.

lead: Testosterone undecanoate injection is a long-acting intramuscular testosterone preparation marketed as Aveed in the United States and Nebido in Europe [1]. It is a prodrug of testosterone used for replacement therapy in adult men with low or absent endogenous testosterone [1].

The FDA rejected Aveed in 2008, 2009 and 2013 over pulmonary oil microembolism and anaphylaxis concerns, then approved it in March 2014 with a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy [1]. Nebido received initial European approval in Finland in November 2003 [1].
Registered studies cover long-term safety in hypogonadal men, blood pressure effects, erectile dysfunction, delayed puberty and others [2][3][4][5]. No studies have examined it for cosmetic outcomes.
infobox: About 21-34 days depending on oil vehicle [1]

paras: The labelled use is testosterone replacement in adult men with hypogonadism [1]. Registered studies have also looked at its use for delayed puberty in boys [6] and combined with PDE-5 inhibitors in hypogonadal men with erectile dysfunction [7].

Reported effects include acne, body-hair growth, increased libido, hypertension, raised liver enzymes and raised triglycerides [1]. A rare risk is pulmonary oil microembolism (POME) after injection, and anaphylaxis has been reported, including a reaction to a benzyl benzoate excipient described in Australia [1]. These concerns led to the US REMS requirement [1].

Ciba filed patents for a related undecylenate combination in the mid-1950s, and injectable undecanoate was used in China before oral products appeared in Europe [1]. Nebido launched in Europe in 2004-2005; after three FDA rejections, Aveed was approved in 2014 [1].
Testosterone undecanoate is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US and Schedule IV in Canada, available by prescription [1].

A phase 3 safety study (NCT00467870) enrolled 531 hypogonadal men receiving intramuscular undecanoate [2]. A phase 4 trial of 673 men examined blood pressure effects of testosterone replacement [3]. A phase 3 trial (n=96) assessed long-term treatment in hypogonadal males [4]. A phase 4 trial of 34 participants tested the drug during military operations with caloric restriction and sleep loss [5], and a small trial examined delayed puberty replacement [6]. A 2025 trial on testosterone-induced muscle memory is recruiting [8]. No studies found examining it for appearance outcomes in healthy people.
